items.stem: What were the small furnaces built during the Great Leap Forward to produce steel called?
items.answer: Backyard furnaces
items.markingKey: Backyard furnaces. Much of the steel produced was useless pig iron.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the First Five-Year Plan and the Great Leap Forward.
items.answer: The First Five-Year Plan followed the Soviet model of centralised planning and expert-led heavy industry; the Great Leap Forward relied on mass mobilisation, communes and revolutionary enthusiasm, rejecting experts, with catastrophic results.
items.markingKey: The First Five-Year Plan followed the Soviet model of centralised planning and expert-led heavy industry; the Great Leap Forward relied on mass mobilisation, communes and revolutionary enthusiasm, rejecting experts, with catastrophic results. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "The Great Leap Forward famine was caused by natural disasters." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: There was some bad weather, but historians such as Frank Dikötter and Yang Jisheng show the famine was mainly caused by policy, false reporting and grain requisitioning.
items.markingKey: There was some bad weather, but historians such as Frank Dikötter and Yang Jisheng show the famine was mainly caused by policy, false reporting and grain requisitioning. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source D
If the Chinese do not begin to work hard, and if we do not achieve our targets for steel, we will lag behind Britain for ever. In fifteen years we will catch up with and overtake Britain in steel production.
— Mao Zedong, speech in Moscow, November 1957, and repeated in party meetings in 1958 (paraphrased)

Outline the message that the author of Source D intended to convey. [2]
items.answer: China must work hard to meet steel targets; failure would leave China behind Britain; China would overtake British steel output within fifteen years.
items.markingKey: China must work hard to meet steel targets; failure would leave China behind Britain; China would overtake British steel output within fifteen years. Award 1 mark for each valid point about the message, up to [2]; a description of the source without interpretation of its message scores at most 1.

items.stem: "Land reform in 1950 was a peaceful redistribution of land." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Land reform was carried out through violent mass struggle meetings; landlords were publicly denounced and many were executed.
items.markingKey: Land reform was carried out through violent mass struggle meetings; landlords were publicly denounced and many were executed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Anti-Rightist Campaign (1957) shows Mao’s consolidation of control over intellectuals.
items.answer: Deng Xiaoping supervised the labelling of over 550,000 people as “rightists”, many sent to labour camps. It silenced critics and made officials afraid to report problems, contributing to the disasters of the Great Leap.
items.markingKey: Context (Deng Xiaoping supervised the labelling of over 550,000 people as “rightists”, many sent to labour camps.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It silenced critics and made officials afraid to report problems, contributing to the disasters of the Great Leap. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to Mao’s consolidation of control over intellectuals.

items.answer: Mao combined mass mobilisation, terror and nationalism to build a powerful party-state by 1957.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. Indicative content: land reform and mass campaigns; Three-Anti and Five-Anti; Korean War and nationalism; Hundred Flowers and Anti-Rightist Campaign. items.stem: To what extent is it true that Mao’s economic policies between 1949 and 1961 were a failure?
items.answer: The First Five-Year Plan had real achievements, but the Great Leap was a catastrophe that outweighed them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the Great Leap Forward famine (30–45 million dead); communes destroyed incentives; industrial output collapsed after 1960. items.stem: Explain why the First Five-Year Plan was considered a success.
items.answer: Industrial output grew by around 16–19 per cent a year, steel production quadrupled to about 5.35 million tonnes and major projects were built with Soviet help, although agriculture lagged behind.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Industrial output grew by around 16–19 per cent a year, steel production quadrupled to about 5.35 million tonnes and major projects were built with Soviet help, although agriculture lagged behind. items.stem: Using the Xinyang incident (1959–1960) as an example, explain the human cost of the Great Leap Forward.
items.answer: In Xinyang prefecture, Henan, officials enforced grain procurement despite starvation; perhaps a million people died. The incident shows how political pressure and false reporting turned policy failure into mass famine.
items.markingKey: Context (In Xinyang prefecture, Henan, officials enforced grain procurement despite starvation; perhaps a million people died.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The incident shows how political pressure and false reporting turned policy failure into mass famine. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the human cost of the Great Leap Forward.

items.stem: Which document, a collection of Mao’s quotations, became a symbol of the Cultural Revolution?
items.answer: The Little Red Book
items.markingKey: The Little Red Book. Lin Biao promoted Quotations from Chairman Mao for the PLA in 1964.

items.stem: Leila writes: "The Cultural Revolution only affected intellectuals in the cities." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It affected all of society: millions of youths were sent to the countryside, officials were purged nationwide and violence occurred in rural areas such as Guangxi.
items.markingKey: It affected all of society: millions of youths were sent to the countryside, officials were purged nationwide and violence occurred in rural areas such as Guangxi. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which head of state was purged and died in detention in 1969?

Liu Shaoqi
Zhou Enlai
Lin Biao
items.answer: Liu Shaoqi
items.markingKey: B. Liu was labelled “China’s Khrushchev”.

items.stem: "The Cultural Revolution was primarily a power struggle within the Chinese Communist Party." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It was both a power struggle and an ideological campaign; Mao used ideology to reclaim power.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: purges of Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping; fall of Lin Biao; Gang of Four versus pragmatists. Arguments against: Mao’s ideological concern about revisionism; mass mobilisation of youth and social upheaval; attacks on culture (Four Olds). Supported judgement: It was both a power struggle and an ideological campaign; Mao used ideology to reclaim power. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Household Responsibility System"?
options: Old customs, culture, habits and ideas, which Red Guards were encouraged to destroy
The Soviet-style plan of 1953–1957 that prioritised heavy industry, with Soviet loans and technical advisers
The official description of Deng’s mixed system combining market reforms with one-party rule
The reform allowing peasant families to lease land and sell surplus produce after meeting state quotas, which replaced collective farming
items.answer: The reform allowing peasant families to lease land and sell surplus produce after meeting state quotas, which replaced collective farming
items.markingKey: D. "Household Responsibility System" is the reform allowing peasant families to lease land and sell surplus produce after meeting state quotas, which replaced collective farming.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Deng Xiaoping introduced economic reforms after 1978.
items.answer: The Cultural Revolution had left the economy backward; Deng believed prosperity would legitimise the party; Asian neighbours (Taiwan, Hong Kong) showed the success of markets; and pragmatism (“It doesn’t matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice”) guided policy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Cultural Revolution had left the economy backward; Deng believed prosperity would legitimise the party; Asian neighbours (Taiwan, Hong Kong) showed the success of markets; and pragmatism (“It doesn’t matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice”) guided policy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between Mao’s economic policy and Deng’s economic policy.
items.answer: Mao favoured collectivisation, self-reliance and mass mobilisation; Deng introduced market incentives, decollectivisation, foreign investment and integration into the world economy, while retaining state control of key sectors.
items.markingKey: Mao favoured collectivisation, self-reliance and mass mobilisation; Deng introduced market incentives, decollectivisation, foreign investment and integration into the world economy, while retaining state control of key sectors. items.stem: "Deng’s reforms introduced democracy to China." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Deng insisted on the Four Cardinal Principles, including the leadership of the Communist Party; economic liberalisation was not matched by political democracy.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the Cultural Revolution was primarily a power struggle within the Chinese Communist Party.
items.answer: It was both a power struggle and an ideological campaign; Mao used ideology to reclaim power.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: purges of Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping; fall of Lin Biao; Gang of Four versus pragmatists. Arguments against: Mao’s ideological concern about revisionism; mass mobilisation of youth and social upheaval; attacks on culture (Four Olds). Supported judgement: It was both a power struggle and an ideological campaign; Mao used ideology to reclaim power. Markbands (10 marks): Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, in-depth accurate knowledge supporting critical analysis, perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – limited understanding of the demands, mainly description.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Agrarian Reform Law (1950)".
items.answer: The law that redistributed land from landlords to peasants, carried out through mass “speak bitterness” meetings in which perhaps one to two million landlords were killed
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the law that redistributed land from landlords to peasants, carried out through mass “speak bitterness” meetings in which perhaps one to two million landlords were killed. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Special Economic Zones (SEZs)"?
options: Areas such as Shenzhen, established from 1980, where foreign investment and market practices were permitted
The reform allowing peasant families to lease land and sell surplus produce after meeting state quotas, which replaced collective farming
The radical leaders Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen, arrested in October 1976
The official description of Deng’s mixed system combining market reforms with one-party rule
items.answer: Areas such as Shenzhen, established from 1980, where foreign investment and market practices were permitted
items.markingKey: A. "Special Economic Zones (SEZs)" is areas such as Shenzhen, established from 1980, where foreign investment and market practices were permitted.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Red Guard phase (1966–68) and the later Cultural Revolution (1969–76).
items.answer: The Red Guard phase involved mass mobilisation, attacks on officials and factional violence; after 1969 the PLA restored order, Lin Biao fell (1971), and politics became a power struggle between radicals and pragmatists such as Zhou Enlai.
items.markingKey: The Red Guard phase involved mass mobilisation, attacks on officials and factional violence; after 1969 the PLA restored order, Lin Biao fell (1971), and politics became a power struggle between radicals and pragmatists such as Zhou Enlai. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between Deng’s political policy and Deng’s economic policy.
items.answer: Economically Deng favoured liberalisation and opening; politically he maintained one-party rule under the Four Cardinal Principles and used repression against dissent, as in 1979 and 1989.
items.markingKey: Economically Deng favoured liberalisation and opening; politically he maintained one-party rule under the Four Cardinal Principles and used repression against dissent, as in 1979 and 1989. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Great Leap Forward caused a famine.
items.answer: Communes and inflated grain targets led officials to report false harvests, so the state requisitioned grain peasants needed; labour was diverted to backyard furnaces and irrigation; Lysenko-inspired techniques (close planting, deep ploughing) cut yields; and fear after Lushan stopped criticism.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Communes and inflated grain targets led officials to report false harvests, so the state requisitioned grain peasants needed; labour was diverted to backyard furnaces and irrigation; Lysenko-inspired techniques (close planting, deep ploughing) cut yields; and fear after Lushan stopped criticism. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between Deng’s economic policy and Mao’s economic policy.
items.answer: Mao favoured collectivisation, self-reliance and mass mobilisation; Deng introduced market incentives, decollectivisation, foreign investment and integration into the world economy, while retaining state control of key sectors.
items.markingKey: Mao favoured collectivisation, self-reliance and mass mobilisation; Deng introduced market incentives, decollectivisation, foreign investment and integration into the world economy, while retaining state control of key sectors. items.stem: Outline one way in which the closure of Democracy Wall (1979) shows the limits of political liberalisation under Deng.
items.answer: After Wei Jingsheng criticised Deng directly, the authorities closed the wall and arrested activists. The episode showed Deng tolerated criticism only when it served his struggle against Maoist rivals.
items.markingKey: Context (After Wei Jingsheng criticised Deng directly, the authorities closed the wall and arrested activists.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Source C
In the commune where I worked, the officials told us to report a harvest of 800 jin per mu when we had harvested less than 200. Then the state took the grain, and by the winter people were eating bark and grass. No one dared to speak.
— Testimony of a former villager in Anhui, recorded in Yang Jisheng, Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958–1962 (2008, English edition 2012) (paraphrased)

Identify three points made in Source C about Mao’s consolidation of power and economic policies, 1949–1961. [3]
items.answer: Officials falsely inflated harvest figures; the state requisitioned grain on the basis of these figures; people starved and ate bark and grass; fear silenced protest.

items.stem: With reference to the growth of Shenzhen (1980–2000), explain how it illustrates the impact of Special Economic Zones.
items.answer: Shenzhen attracted foreign investment from Hong Kong, growing into a major manufacturing and export centre. Shenzhen demonstrated the benefits of opening up and became a model for coastal development.
items.markingKey: Context (Shenzhen attracted foreign investment from Hong Kong, growing into a major manufacturing and export centre.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Shenzhen demonstrated the benefits of opening up and became a model for coastal development. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the impact of Special Economic Zones.

According to Source A, what can be learned about the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976)? [3]
items.answer: Red Guards humiliated teachers as reactionaries; they believed they were defending Mao; later the speaker felt they had been manipulated.

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source B, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating political change and repression in the PRC, 1978–1989. [4]
items.answer: Value: It is a contemporary image that became a global symbol of the crackdown and shaped international perceptions. Limitations: It shows a single moment after the massacre and does not show the violence of 3–4 June; its meaning has been shaped by Western media.

items.stem: With reference to the period and region you have studied in depth: Discuss the impact of the Cultural Revolution on Chinese society. [15]
items.answer: The Cultural Revolution devastated society, but its failures created support for reform after 1978.
items.markingKey: Paper 3 essay. Indicative content: education disrupted and youth sent down; cultural destruction; deaths and persecution; disillusionment that paved the way for Deng’s reforms.
